Where is Wichita, Kansas, and how big is it?

Wichita is the most populous city in Kansas and the county seat of Sedgwick County, in south-central Kansas along the Arkansas River. The 2020 census counted 397,532 residents in the city and 647,610 in the metro area.

The city grew from a trading post on the Chisholm Trail in the 1860s, was incorporated in 1870, and later became the cattle-drive stop nicknamed Cowtown. In the 1920s and 1930s aircraft makers such as Beechcraft, Cessna and Stearman set up shop, and the city still calls itself the Air Capital of the World.

What drives the Wichita economy?

Aircraft manufacturing leads, followed by schools, the military, health care and a few large private companies. The Greater Wichita Partnership's employer list, updated September 2026, shows the following approximate headcounts.

  • The Boeing Company (aircraft assemblies): 13,000
  • Textron Aviation (Beechcraft and Cessna): 11,000
  • Wichita USD 259: 9,100
  • McConnell Air Force Base: 6,000
  • Wichita State University: 5,500
  • City of Wichita: 3,400
  • Ascension Via Christi, Wesley Healthcare and Koch: roughly 3,000 to 3,300 each

The partnership notes that Cargill Protein and Koch Industries, the two largest privately held companies in the U.S., both have a presence in the region. Those employers are a useful reference point when you describe commute distances to a buyer.

What does Wichita's weather mean for a house?

Wichita gets severe spring storms with large hail and frequent lightning, and tornadoes have struck the area several times, including in September 1965, April 1991 and May 1999. Roofs, gutters, windows and siding take the brunt of it.

Flooding is the other local history. The Arkansas River flooded Wichita in 1877, 1904, 1916, 1923, 1944, 1951 and 1955, and the city flooded three times in 11 days in 1944. That led to the Wichita-Valley Center Floodway, locally called the Big Ditch, finished in 1958. It diverts part of the river around west-central Wichita, roughly parallel to I-235.

Sedgwick County's environmental staff say any activity inside a mapped floodplain in Wichita needs permission, and they point owners to the county floodplain maps and to its floodplain page. Before selling, check whether your parcel falls in a Special Flood Hazard Area, because buyers, lenders and insurers will.

What are Wichita's property maintenance and nuisance rules?

Wichita treats lawn grass and weeds taller than 12 inches as a nuisance, and its adopted International Property Maintenance Code lets the city abate violations and bill the owner when notices are ignored. The city's planning department handles enforcement through the Codes and Regulations enforcement page, where complaints can be reported by phone at 316-268-4421.

The city code defines premises nuisances to include weeds or vines over twelve inches on a property and in the streets and alleys in front of it, along with tree waste. The IPMC also makes each day of an uncorrected violation a separate offense, and it gives the city authority to enter and abate after the notice period passes and charge the costs to the owner.

Chapter 30.01 adds a registry of neglected buildings and dwellings. An owner who receives written notice must register within 30 days, a registration does not transfer to a new owner, and the owner of a registered property must tell the city within ten business days of a sale or transfer. The city posted a November 2025 draft amendment that would raise the registration fee from $25 to $100, so confirm the current figure with the department before relying on either number.

How does Wichita's neglected building registry affect an inherited or vacant house?

A vacant Wichita house can land on the registry if it is unsecured, has fire, wind or water damage that makes it uninhabitable, has been boarded for more than 90 days, or has shown substantial deterioration. Two or more complaints filed in municipal court within 18 months for code violations can also trigger it.

That list matters for estates. A house that sits empty for a few months after a death, with a broken window or storm damage, can drift into a category the city monitors. Owners who live more than 60 miles from the city must name a resident agent within 60 miles of the city limits, according to the draft text, so out-of-area heirs should plan for that.

When does Sedgwick County value property and collect tax?

Sedgwick County mails valuation notices March 1, and the informal appeal form must come back within 30 days, typically March 31. Taxes are due December 20 for the first half or the full amount and May 10 for the second half, according to the county appraiser's appeals page.

A property value can be appealed only once per tax year, through the informal appeal or a payment under protest. If you disagree with the informal result, you may go to the Board of Tax Appeals small claims division for a single-family residence, and you must file within 30 days of the results being mailed. The county suggests bringing comparable sales, a private appraisal, dated photographs of damage, signed repair estimates or an inspection report. For a house that needs work, those condition records can support a lower value.

How are deeds recorded in Sedgwick County?

The Sedgwick County Register of Deeds records deeds and charges fees set by K.S.A. 28-115. Its 2026 schedule lists $21 for the first page of a deed or mortgage and $17 for each additional page, and it says no mortgage tax has been collected since January 1, 2019.

The office cannot quote an exact fee by phone because the final amount depends on inspecting the document. It recommends bringing cash or a card, or leaving a check amount blank until you meet the cashier. In a cash sale the title company records the deed, and Kansas also expects a sales validation questionnaire or a stated exemption with the deed under K.S.A. 79-1437c.

What do Wichita sellers commonly face?

The common problems are storm-damaged roofs, older houses near plants and corridors, inherited property and tenants. A cash buyer can often work around those issues without waiting for a lender's appraisal or repair list.

  • Storm damage: document hail or wind damage before it spreads to the interior.
  • Floodplain parcels: pull the county map early so there are no surprises at closing.
  • Vacant heirs' houses: keep the property secured and mowed to stay clear of the nuisance rules.
  • Tax timing: a December 20 or May 10 bill near closing needs a plan.

Whichever route you pick, gather your latest Sedgwick County tax statement, any code notice and the names on the deed first.

The first half or the full amount is due December 20, and the second half is due May 10. No second statement is mailed if the bill is paid in full by December 20.

What is the deadline to appeal a Wichita property value?

The informal appeal form is due within 30 days of the March 1 notice, which the county says is typically March 31. A property value can be appealed only once per tax year.

How tall can grass get in Wichita before it is a violation?

Over 12 inches is a violation under the city's adopted property maintenance code, and the nuisance rules also cover weeds in the street and alley in front of the property. If the notice is ignored, the city can abate it and charge the owner.

Is my Wichita house in a floodplain?

Check the Sedgwick County floodplain maps, linked from the county's floodplain page. The county says activity inside mapped floodplains in Wichita needs permission, and you can call 316-660-1840 for details.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Sedgwick County?

The 2026 fee schedule lists $21 for the first page and $17 for each additional page. The register says the final fee is set when the document is inspected.

What should you know before selling a house in Overland Park, KS?

The city spans nearly the full north to south length of the county. Houses in different parts of the city can sit in different school districts. The sections below cover what the city requires, what the county does and what the paperwork looks like.

Where does Overland Park sit in the Kansas City metro?

Overland Park lies in northeastern Kansas at the junction of Interstate 435 and US-69, immediately east of Olathe, and its center is about 13 miles south-southwest of downtown Kansas City, Missouri. It covers 75.37 square miles and borders Kansas City, Kansas; Mission; Prairie Village; Leawood; Stilwell; Olathe; Lenexa; Shawnee; and Merriam.

The part of the city north of 159th Street is known as Shawnee Mission. Turkey Creek crosses the far north, and most of the city drains to the Blue River through creeks including Indian Creek and Tomahawk Creek. Interstate 435 and US-50 run east and west through the middle of town, Interstate 35 touches the northwest, and Shawnee Mission Parkway carries US-56 and US-169 across the north. Johnson County Transit, branded The JO, connects Overland Park to other suburbs and to downtown Kansas City, and Kansas City International Airport is about 22 miles north.

How did Overland Park develop?

William B. Strang Jr. arrived in 1905 and began platting subdivisions along an old military road that became the city's main thoroughfare. Overland Park was incorporated as a city of the first class on May 20, 1960, with 28,085 residents.

Growth was fast: 111,790 people by 1990, 149,080 in 2000 and 173,372 in 2010. It passed Kansas City, Kansas in the early 2000s to become the state's second largest city. The city's last attempted annexation, in 2008, drew heavy opposition, and later state law requires a majority vote of affected residents for annexations of more than 40 acres.

Which school districts serve Overland Park?

Four public districts serve the city. Shawnee Mission School District covers the area north of Interstate 435, Blue Valley USD 229 covers most of the city south of it, Olathe Public Schools has two elementary schools in the western part, and Spring Hill covers the extreme southwest.

Both Shawnee Mission and Blue Valley are headquartered in the city. The district for your address is a basic fact buyers check, so confirm it from the district rather than relying on a neighbor or a listing description. More than a dozen private and parochial schools, including St. Thomas Aquinas High School, also operate in the city.

What drives the Overland Park economy?

Services dominate. Health care, retail, professional and technical services, finance and insurance, and information technology are the five largest industries, and Black and Veatch, Ash Grove Cement and Compass Minerals are headquartered here. T-Mobile, which absorbed Sprint in the 2020 merger, is listed as the largest employer.

The city's 2016 financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, put T-Mobile first with 6,300 employees, followed by Shawnee Mission School District, Blue Valley School District, Black and Veatch and Johnson County Community College.

  • Overland Park Regional Medical Center and AdventHealth South Overland Park are among four hospitals in the city.
  • Johnson County Community College and several satellite campuses, including University of Kansas Edwards Campus, are in the city.
  • Oak Park Mall, Topgolf and the Overland Park Convention Center anchor retail and events.

How do utilities and trash service work in Overland Park?

Evergy supplies electricity, Atmos Energy and Kansas Gas Service supply natural gas, and WaterOne provides water. Johnson County Wastewater handles sewer treatment, and the city permits private trash haulers instead of running its own collection.

That last point matters when you move out. Trash service is arranged with a hauler, so a seller should confirm the contract and cancel or transfer it as part of the move, and keep copies of the last bills for the buyer.

What does Overland Park's rental license mean for a seller?

Overland Park requires a rental license for every rental property, including short-term rentals, and the license is not transferable under chapter 5.75 of the city code. A buyer who intends to rent the house must apply in their own name.

The city also inspects the exterior of licensed rentals for compliance with the property maintenance code. A seller who rents out a house should confirm the license is current and resolve any open exterior violations before listing or accepting an offer.

  • Check that the license covers the address and has not lapsed.
  • Tell any buyer that the license does not transfer with the house.
  • Gather inspection notices and repair records.

How does Overland Park handle code complaints?

Code compliance in Overland Park starts after the city receives a complaint. The residential property maintenance page says residents must keep homes and properties to code, and it lists commonly reported issues and a checklist to help owners spot problems.

The property maintenance code is chapter 7.25 of the municipal code. It addresses items such as exterior walls, and it allows the code official to act if an owner does not fix a violation after notice. Sellers of homes with deferred maintenance should look at the checklist before listing.

Which transfers skip the Kansas sales validation questionnaire?

Most deeds need the questionnaire, but K.S.A. 79-1437e lists 16 exemptions. They include gifts, transfers to or from a trust without consideration, divorce settlements, sheriff's deeds, deeds in escrow for more than five years, quit claim deeds filed to clear title, eminent domain conveyances, and transfers by a guardian or executor under court order.

When an exemption applies, it must be clearly stated on the deed itself, and the register of deeds cannot add it at filing. The form also warns that falsifying the value of transferred real estate is a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $500, so a truthful price on the questionnaire matters.

How do Johnson County taxes and deed filing affect an Overland Park closing?

The county treasury says taxes may be paid in full by December 20 or in two installments. Valuation notices go out by March 1, and the appeals page describes an informal appeal as the first step. Payment-under-protest applications are due December 20, January 31 for mortgage-paid accounts, or May 10 for second-half or late full payments.

Deeds are recorded at the Register of Deeds at 111 S. Cherry St. in Olathe, which does not accept email or fax. The deed must be followed immediately by the completed questionnaire. A title company normally handles both steps.

A cash sale can suit an owner with a rental license problem, a house that needs repairs, an estate, or a deadline that a financed buyer cannot meet. A listing may suit a house in turnkey condition in a sought-after district. Call or text and we will give you a straight comparison for your address.

Yes, if the house is rented. The city requires a rental license for all rental properties, including short-term rentals, and the license is not transferable to a new owner.

Which school district serves my Overland Park house?

It depends on the address. Shawnee Mission serves the area north of Interstate 435, Blue Valley serves most of the city south of it, and small western and southwestern areas fall in Olathe and Spring Hill districts.

Who provides water in Overland Park?

WaterOne provides water, and Johnson County Wastewater manages sewer service. Trash service is arranged with private haulers that the city permits.

Where do I record a deed for an Overland Park house?

The Johnson County Register of Deeds records deeds, at 111 S. Cherry St., Suite 1200 in Olathe. Recording by email or fax is not accepted.

What if my deed qualifies for an exemption from the sales questionnaire?

The exemption must be stated on the deed. K.S.A. 79-1437e lists 16, including gifts, sheriff's deeds and transfers by an executor under court order.

Where is Kansas City, Kansas, and how big is it?

Kansas City, Kansas sits at the meeting of the Missouri and Kansas (Kaw) rivers, across the state line from Kansas City, Missouri. It is the largest city on this list by a wide margin: the Census Bureau estimates 157,805 residents as of July 1, 2025, and the city covers 128.38 square miles, of which 124.81 are land.

In 1997 voters approved a proposition to unify the city and Wyandotte County governments, creating the Unified Government of Wyandotte County and Kansas City, Kansas. A sale here therefore involves one combined government for building and rental rules, and a county register of deeds for the recording.

The county register of deeds works from the Wyandotte County Courthouse at 710 N. 7th Street.

How was Kansas City, Kansas formed, and why does that matter for a house?

Kansas City, Kansas was formed in March 1886 by consolidating five municipalities: Kansas City, Armstrong, Armourdale, Riverview and Wyandotte. It grew fast in the 1890s as a streetcar suburb of Kansas City, Missouri, and passed 100,000 residents in 1920.

Argentine joined in 1910 and Rosedale in 1922. Because the city grew by merging separate towns, house age and style vary a great deal from one neighborhood to the next.

  • Armourdale, Riverview, Armstrong and Wyandotte were separate towns before the 1886 merger, and each kept its own street pattern and building history.
  • Argentine, named for a silver smelter, and Rosedale were once separate towns.
  • Piper and Turner have their own school districts, USD 203 and USD 202.
  • Maywood has become part of the Village West district, which includes the Legends shopping area, Kansas Speedway and the Sporting Kansas City stadium.

Older housing can come with older wiring, plumbing and foundations, which is a common cause of pre-sale repair bills.

What are the major employers, and who buys houses here?

Health care leads the employer list. Wikipedia, citing the city's annual financial report, lists the University of Kansas Health System first, then the University of Kansas Medical Center and Amazon fulfillment centers, followed by Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools, UPS, the Unified Government, BNSF Railway, Urban Outfitters, General Motors and Providence Medical Center.

General Motors runs the Fairfax Assembly Plant in the Fairfax District along the Missouri River. Associated Wholesale Grocers and Kansas City Steak Company are also based in the city.

With such large employers inside the city and the metro, buyers include hospital staff, warehouse and rail workers. A seller does not need to know every buyer, but knowing where demand comes from helps you judge an offer.

What do Census numbers say about Kansas City, Kansas housing?

About 61 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and the median home value is $167,400, according to the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates.

Does Kansas City, Kansas require a rental license?

Yes. The Rental Licensing and Inspection program began in 1996 and requires every landlord of residential rental property to keep a valid rental license. All licenses expire on April 30 each year, and the property owner is responsible for getting one.

The Neighborhood Resource Center, 4953 State Avenue, handles the program at (913) 573-8649. The city's tenant checklist shows what inspectors look for:

  • Smoke detectors in each bedroom and on each level.
  • GFCI outlets in bathrooms.
  • Handrails at stairs with four or more risers.
  • Operable windows that are not blocked or boarded.
  • A vented, working furnace and water heater.
  • Safe electrical panels and circuits.

If you own a rental you plan to sell, confirm that the license is current and that no open violations exist. A buyer's lender or an investor may check.

How are deeds recorded in Wyandotte County?

Deeds are recorded at the Wyandotte County Register of Deeds, which is open Monday through Friday. The office lists a recording fee of $21 for the first page and $17 for each additional page of a deed or mortgage, with fees on a single-family mortgage on a principal residence capped at $125 when the debt is $75,000 or less and an affidavit is provided.

  • Every deed must be signed and properly notarized, name the grantor and grantee, and carry the legal description.
  • A deed must come with a real estate sales validation questionnaire, or state an exemption under K.S.A. 79-1437e.
  • The notary certificate must be complete, including the date, the county and state, the seal and the commission expiration date, or the office will reject the document.
  • The office cannot draft documents, give legal advice or run a title search, and recommends an attorney or title company.

The office also notes that the sales price is not public record in Kansas under K.S.A. 79-1437f. Foreclosure suits are filed in district court, not at the register of deeds, and the office does not track them while pending.

How does weather and flooding risk affect a Kansas City, Kansas house?

Kansas City is in a humid continental climate zone with four distinct seasons, USDA plant hardiness zone 6, and big swings between hot and cold because it is far from any large body of water. Summers can be hot and moderately humid when Gulf air moves in.

The city lies at the confluence of the Missouri and Kansas rivers. If your house is near a river valley or creek, check its flood zone on the FEMA map before you list, and keep any insurance records.

Roofs, gutters and drainage are the most common weather-related items a buyer's inspector notes in this climate.

How do roads, schools and transit work in Kansas City, Kansas?

Interstates 70, 35, 435, 635 and 670 all pass through or around the city, along with K-5, K-7, K-32 and U.S. 24 and 40. A portion of I-70 here was the first project in the country completed under the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956.

  • RideKC is the local transit provider, and Greyhound uses the 47th Street Transit Center.
  • Kansas City International Airport is the nearest airport, and Amtrak runs from Kansas City Union Station across the state line.
  • Public schools are in Kansas City USD 500, Piper USD 203 and Turner USD 202, and the city has Kansas City Kansas Community College and Donnelly College.

The mean commute is 22.4 minutes, so highway access and distance to downtown Kansas City, Missouri, the medical center or Village West are real selling points.

What do Kansas City, Kansas sellers usually face?

Sellers here tend to have one of these situations, and each calls for a different plan:

  • Landlords. A rental license, open housing violations or a tenant who will not leave complicates a regular listing.
  • Estates. The register of deeds requires proper notarization, which can be slow with heirs in other states.
  • Older house repairs. Older housing can need major work that some lenders will not finance.
  • Short timelines. A relocation or a lender deadline leaves little room for repairs and showings.

A cash buyer will usually inspect the house as it is, make a written offer and close at a title company. Keep your own numbers for the comparison: agent commission and repair costs on a listing, and the days the house may sit unsold.

Does Kansas City, KS require landlords to have a rental license?

Yes. The Unified Government's Rental Licensing and Inspection program, begun in 1996, requires a valid license for every residential rental. Licenses expire each April 30.

Where do I record a deed in Kansas City, KS?

At the Wyandotte County Register of Deeds in the Wyandotte County Courthouse, 710 N. 7th Street, Suite 100. The deed must be notarized, include the legal description, and come with a sales validation questionnaire or a stated exemption.

Can the register of deeds tell me if my title is clear?

No. The office says it cannot give legal advice, draft documents or give an opinion on title. A title company or abstractor searches the records and court files to check for liens and other claims.

Is the sale price of a Kansas City, KS house public record?

No. The Wyandotte County Register of Deeds says sales price is not public record in Kansas under K.S.A. 79-1437f, even though the deed is recorded.

John T. Barton founded Olathe in the spring of 1857, and the town was named the Johnson County seat in October 1859. Local lore says the name came from a Shawnee word for beautiful.

The early town lived off travelers on the Santa Fe, Oregon and California trails. The Mahaffie House, a wagon resupply point, is now a historic site run by the city. On September 6, 1862, William Quantrill's guerrillas raided Olathe and destroyed most of the town. The town then stayed small for decades.

Interstate 35 changed that in the 1950s by linking Olathe to Kansas City, Missouri. The census counts show the result: 10,987 people in 1960, 37,258 in 1980, 92,962 in 2000 and 141,290 in 2020. That is about 130,000 added residents in 60 years.

Olathe covers 60.42 square miles and borders Lenexa to the north, Overland Park to the east, De Soto to the northwest and Gardner to the southwest. Two public lakes sit inside the city: Lake Olathe at 172 acres of water and Cedar Lake at 45 acres.

Johnson County Transit runs a bus system through the county, including Olathe. A BNSF main line passes through the city. Johnson County Executive Airport, on about 500 acres with a 4,100-foot runway, is the second busiest airport in the state, and the closest airport with airline service is Kansas City International. The Federal Aviation Administration also operates the Kansas City air route traffic control center in Olathe.

Garmin, Olathe Public Schools, Olathe Health System, Johnson County Government and Farmers Insurance head the list in the city's 2022 financial report as summarized on Wikipedia. Honeywell, TransAm Trucking and the FAA also appear.

Farmers Insurance is based in Los Angeles, but Olathe has more of its employees than any other city in the United States. Olathe Public Schools says on its own site that it is a Forbes-recognized top employer.

Which school districts serve Olathe houses?

Five public districts reach into Olathe: Olathe USD 233, De Soto USD 232, Spring Hill USD 230, Blue Valley USD 229 and Gardner-Edgerton USD 231. Olathe USD 233 operates five high schools: Olathe North, South, East, Northwest and West.

If you live near a district line, the district named on your address matters to a buyer who is comparing homes. Check the district for your parcel before you describe it to anyone. MidAmerica Nazarene University and the Kansas School for the Deaf, founded in 1861, are also in Olathe.

What does Olathe's weather do to a house?

Olathe has a humid continental climate, with a January average high near 39 degrees and a July average high near 90. The temperature reaches 90 degrees about 36 days a year and 100 degrees about three days, and it falls below freezing on about 102 days.

Precipitation averages about 40 inches a year, most of it in May and June, and snowfall averages about 19 inches. The city's exterior maintenance code lists roofs, exterior surfaces, gutters, doors and windows among the items that must be kept in good condition, so a roof that has aged badly is both a buyer concern and a code issue.

What do Olathe's code and permit rules mean for a seller?

Olathe's Community Enhancement Division inspects properties for exterior code violations, and the city lists specific limits owners should know before showing a house.

  • Dead or diseased trees must come down, and limbs must stay above 13.5 feet over a street and 10 feet over a sidewalk.
  • Inoperable vehicles may not be stored outside, and tarps may not cover a vehicle.
  • Trash carts go to the curb after 5 p.m. the day before pickup and come in before 5 p.m. the next day.

After a complaint, an officer inspects, notifies the owner and sets a compliance time frame, which can be extended on request. If the owner does not comply, the city can abate the problem or send a notice to appear in Municipal Court. A seller with an open violation should clear it before closing so it does not pass to the buyer.

The residential permit page also says permits are not required for reroofing or for repairs down to the roof deck on one-family and two-family dwellings and townhomes, although the work must meet the current International Residential Code and the Olathe code. That helps an owner who wants to replace a roof before listing.

What should an Olathe landlord handle before selling?

Landlords selling in Olathe have a utility step to handle. The city says landlords on the automatic utility transfer program must call 913-971-9311 to cancel it if the property is sold, so the account does not keep reverting to the former owner.

Short-term rental hosts are asked to be considerate of neighbors, check any homeowners' association rules and follow city noise, trash and property maintenance codes. If the house is in an HOA, confirm those rules before you promise a buyer that a rental plan is allowed.

The city sits where I-70 meets U.S. Highway 75, and it is the starting point of I-335, the stretch of the Kansas Turnpike that runs to Emporia. A house near an interchange, a rail line or the Oakland Expressway can show differently to buyers than one on a quiet interior street, so a seller does well to describe the real location instead of a generic one.

Topeka was laid out in 1854 and chartered as a city in 1857. Construction of the Kansas State Capitol began in 1866, and the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railroad opened its general offices and machine shops there in 1878. State government, health care, schools, finance and food or consumer manufacturing make up most of Topeka's large employers. A seller can mention nearby employers in a conversation with a buyer. An incentive like this does not change what a given house is worth, so confirm the program terms directly if a buyer brings it up.

Topeka enforces the International Property Maintenance Code through its Property Maintenance Unit, and an unresolved violation stays with the property when it changes hands. The unit works from 620 SE Madison and takes complaints by phone at 785-368-3161, by email or through SeeClickFix.

According to the city's property ownership and maintenance page, a code official schedules an inspection within 48 hours of a complaint. The city lists these best-case timelines when an owner does not comply voluntarily:

  • Weeds: 14 days, with vegetation over 12 inches prohibited.
  • Inoperable vehicles: 21 days, then towing.
  • Sanitation: 21 days, covering trash, tires, mattresses, appliances and similar items left outside.
  • Housing violations: 4 to 6 months.
  • Unsafe structures: 6 to 12 months.

If a violation is not fixed, the city can abate it and bill the owner for the work plus administrative and penalty fees. An owner who disagrees can ask for an administrative hearing, which the city holds twice a month. The city says about 30 to 40 structures are demolished each year, by the city or by the owner, so a badly deteriorated house can end up in that process.

Topeka requires owners of properties vacant for more than 180 days to register them, under Chapter 8.65 of the city code adopted in November 2019. The Property Maintenance Unit sends a notice to owners it determines are vacant, and an owner who disagrees can file a dispute with the city.

This hits inherited houses and out-of-town owners most often. If you are holding an empty Topeka house while an estate settles, check whether you have received a registration notice and answer it, because a sale usually goes faster when the city file is clean.

Short-term rentals in Topeka need an administrative permit in most residential zones, and the permit lasts two years. Topeka divides them into three types: Type I for owner-occupied homes, Type II for non-owner-occupied homes and Type III for homes with six or more guest bedrooms.

The city also bans landlords from retaliating against a tenant who complains in good faith about housing conditions. Under Topeka Municipal Code 9.25.020, evicting a tenant, raising rent or cutting services within six months of such a complaint is unlawful, while eviction for unpaid rent or lease violations remains allowed. A seller with a tenant in place should keep those limits in mind when planning the timing of a sale.

Deeds are recorded by the Shawnee County Register of Deeds, which lists $21.00 for the first page of a deed, mortgage or other instrument. The county fee schedule also adds $1.00 if signer or notary names are not plainly typed or printed under the signatures.

Kansas registers of deeds also require a real estate sales validation questionnaire with a deed, or a clearly stated exemption on the deed, under K.S.A. 79-1437c and 79-1437e. The title company normally prepares that form, but a seller can help by giving exact legal names and confirming how the owner or owners hold title.

The common cases are older houses needing work, inherited property, tenant situations and code violations that have been piling up. A cash buyer can take on those conditions where a conventional buyer's lender may not.

Where is Lawrence, Kansas, and what does the city look like?

Lawrence is a Douglas County city about 25 miles east of Topeka and 35 miles west of Kansas City, Kansas. It sits between the Kansas River and the Wakarusa River, which shapes both its streets and its flood maps.

The Census Bureau puts the city at 34.26 square miles, with the highest ground on Mount Oread, where the University of Kansas campus stands at 1,020 feet. Several creeks cross town. Burroughs Creek runs through East Lawrence, Baldwin Creek drains the northwest, and Yankee Tank Creek in the southwest feeds Lake Alvamar before reaching the Wakarusa.

Lawrence also has 54 parks and a planned 22-mile Lawrence Loop trail that circles the city. For a seller, that mix of campus, river valley and park land means two houses a mile apart can sit in very different settings, and buyers notice it.

What is the history behind Lawrence houses?

Lawrence was founded in 1854 by antislavery settlers, so some of its housing stock is among the oldest in Kansas. On August 21, 1863, William Quantrill's raiders destroyed most of the town's houses and businesses, so the oldest surviving buildings mostly come from the rebuilding that followed.

Older neighborhoods close to downtown, such as Old West Lawrence, North Lawrence, East Lawrence, Oread, Hancock and Pinkney, tend to hold older homes. Farther west, past Iowa Street, are Sunset Hills, Prairie Meadows, Deerfield and Alvamar. Age matters when you sell. An older house may carry original wiring, plumbing or a stone foundation, and a conventional buyer's lender and inspector will ask about each of them.

What drives the Lawrence economy and housing demand?

Education is the center of the local economy. The University of Kansas was the largest employer in the city as of 2020, with 10,116 employees, followed by Maximus, Lawrence Memorial Hospital and Hallmark Cards.

A university town has a housing rhythm of its own. Leases tend to turn over in summer, and the city's own rental inspection rules reflect that: Lawrence does not schedule required rental inspections in July or August unless the owner asks. If you own a rental near campus, the calendar can affect when a vacant house is easiest to show or hand over.

The city also had a rise in homelessness after 2019, and in February 2023 the City Commission passed an ordinance banning source of income discrimination, so landlords cannot turn away housing vouchers. Landlords thinking of selling a tenant-occupied house should know that rule exists.

Which roads and transit connect Lawrence to the rest of the region?

Interstate 70, which runs here as the Kansas Turnpike, crosses the northern edge of the city. U.S. 59 runs north and south along Iowa Street, and U.S. 40 follows 6th Street. K-10 reaches Kansas City by way of the South Lawrence Trafficway, which was connected in November 2016, and the Kansas Department of Transportation began widening the western stretch to four lanes in 2024.

Two bus systems serve the city: Lawrence Transit, known as The T, and KU on Wheels. Together they run 18 routes. Kansas City International Airport is roughly 50 miles northeast of downtown. The commute to the Kansas City area is one reason some owners keep a Lawrence house for years, and one reason a buyer may accept a longer drive for a lower price.

What is the climate in Lawrence, and what does it do to a house?

Lawrence has a humid continental climate with hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters. The table below uses 1991 to 2020 normals from the long Lawrence record.

Wide swings between a freezing winter and a hot summer also stress siding, driveways and foundations. Those are the items a buyer's inspector writes up first, so they are also the items that drag a conventional sale into repair negotiations.

Do Lawrence rental licensing rules affect a sale?

Yes, if the house is rented. Lawrence requires a license for every rental dwelling unit in the city, renewed each year, under Ordinance 8840, adopted April 1, 2014.

The city's FAQ lists several points that matter to an owner who wants out:

  • Vacant rental units must still be licensed.
  • A house under contract to be bought by its tenant stays on the licensing rolls until the buyer's name is recorded with the Douglas County Register of Deeds.
  • If the owner lives elsewhere and a relative lives in the house, it is exempt. If that relative has an unrelated roommate, it must be licensed.
  • Required inspections run on a 3-year or 6-year cycle depending on how many violations were found, and the owner or agent must attend.
  • A notice of violation generally gives 30 days to fix items, and an appeal goes to the Building Code Board of Appeals within 14 days.

Failing to license a rental before renting it may be prosecuted in municipal court. Occupancy limits also matter: the city's zoning rules allow up to three unrelated occupants in single-family districts and four in most other districts. An investor or an heir who inherits a rental with an expired license or open violations can find that a normal listing stalls. A buyer who takes the house as-is does not need the license fixed before closing.

What should a Lawrence seller know about taxes and the county offices?

Property tax in Lawrence is billed by Douglas County. The county treasurer's office is at 2601 West 6th Street, and the Register of Deeds is in the county courthouse at 1100 Massachusetts Street.

The Douglas County Treasurer explains the residential formula this way: appraised value times 11.5 percent gives assessed value, and assessed value times the mill levy, divided by 1,000, gives the estimated tax. The first half of the tax bill is due on or before December 20, and the treasurer takes calls at 785-832-5178 for tax questions.

At closing, the title company normally prorates the year's tax between buyer and seller, so ask for a payoff and proration figure early. If taxes are behind, the treasurer's page on tax foreclosures shows how the county handles them.

How does recording a deed work in Douglas County?

The Douglas County Register of Deeds records deeds, mortgages, plats and other real estate documents, and a title company or attorney generally handles the filing for a sale.

The office accepts electronic recordings from four named vendors: Simplifile, Mobilis, CSC and ePN. Documents for property in the county must carry the full legal description, and the office advises against abbreviated descriptions. The county publishes a Kansas Real Estate Sales Validation Questionnaire, which is part of how a sale price is reported.

The office does not prepare deeds and recommends that a title company or attorney do it, since a drafting error can change ownership in ways that are costly to fix. It also runs a free Real Estate Fraud Alert service: you enroll by name and get an email when a matching name is indexed. An owner who inherited a Lawrence house, or who lives out of town, may find that useful while the property sits vacant.

What are the main ways to sell a house in Lawrence?

There are three practical routes: list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is.

  • Listing: best when the house is in good shape and you can wait through showings, inspection requests and a buyer's loan approval.
  • Selling yourself: saves an agent's fee but puts marketing, disclosures and paperwork on you.
  • Cash offer: suits a vacant rental, an inherited house, a property with code violations or a seller who needs a firm closing date.

In Lawrence, cash tends to come up with student rentals that need work after a hard lease year, with inherited houses in older neighborhoods, and with owners who live elsewhere. Whatever the route, compare the net figure after repairs, carrying costs and time, not only the headline number. We buy houses in Lawrence as-is, and you can request an offer without obligation.

Do I need a rental license to sell a rented house in Lawrence?

You need the license to keep renting, but not to sell. Lawrence requires a license for each rental unit, including vacant ones, until a buyer's name is recorded as owner with the Douglas County Register of Deeds. Letting a license lapse while tenants remain can bring municipal court action.

When are Douglas County property taxes due?

The first half or the full amount is due on or before December 20. The Douglas County Treasurer receives payments after November 1, and tax questions go to 785-832-5178.

Where is a deed recorded for a Lawrence house?

At the Douglas County Register of Deeds, 1100 Massachusetts Street in Lawrence. Title companies usually record electronically through a vendor such as Simplifile, so the seller seldom files the deed personally.

Does the University of Kansas affect when a house sells?

It affects rentals most. The university is the city's largest employer, summer is the busy lease turnover period, and the city does not schedule required rental inspections in July or August unless the owner requests one.

Can I sell a Lawrence house with code or inspection problems?

Yes. A cash buyer purchases as-is, so open violations, deferred repairs or a failed rental inspection do not have to be fixed first. A conventional buyer's lender and inspector will usually require those items to be addressed.

The answer depends on the address, because the City of Shawnee says it is served by two public districts, Shawnee Mission (USD 512) and De Soto (USD 232). A few private schools also operate inside the city.

This matters at sale time for a practical reason: the district sets a large share of the tax bill. A buyer comparing two Shawnee houses will see different total levies depending on which district the parcel falls in, and a seller who knows the district can explain the bill before the buyer asks.

The city's 2027 budget presentation lists two combined mill rates for 2026 budget-year levies: 106.066 mills in the Shawnee Mission district and 117.222 mills in the De Soto district. The city's own levy is 23.267 mills in both, and the proposal for 2027 left it flat.

When are Johnson County property values set and taxes due?

Johnson County values every parcel as of January 1, mails Notices of Appraised Value on or before March 1, and bills real estate tax on November 15. The county appraiser keeps the full calendar on its important dates page.

  • January 1: valuation date for the appraisal year.
  • On or before March 1: valuation notices mailed to real property owners.
  • On or before March 31: appeal deadline, set at 30 days after the notice mailing date.
  • May 1: second-half bills mailed.
  • May 15: informal-level real property appeals completed.
  • May 20: last day for appeal decisions to be mailed.
  • November 15: tax bills mailed.
  • December 20: first half, or the full amount, due.

If you sell in the spring, the second half usually arrives in the middle of your closing plans. Ask the title company how it will handle the unpaid portion before you set a closing date.

How do I appeal a Shawnee home valuation?

You appeal to the Johnson County Appraiser, not to the city. The county offers an informal appeal when the notice arrives and a payment under protest when you pay the bill, and you may use only one of the two in a tax year.

Applications go through the county's online appeal portal, or by mail to the Appraiser's Office in Olathe. A hearing is required, and the county lets you choose between evidence only, a 20-minute phone call or a 20-minute in-person meeting. A payment under protest application is due December 20 if you pay the bill yourself, January 31 if a mortgage company pays it, and May 10 for second-half or late full payments. If you disagree with the result, you have 30 days from the mailing date to go to the Kansas State Board of Tax Appeals. The county notes that its appraisers must visit each property at least once every six years, and that a structural problem such as a foundation crack can lower a value.

What permits and yard rules affect selling a house in Shawnee?

Shawnee requires permits for structural work, electrical upgrades, demolitions, pools and hot tubs, but not for cosmetic interior updates. The city's building permits FAQ lists the common cases, which helps when you are deciding what to fix before a sale.

  • Cabinets, doors, windows, carpet and plumbing fixtures: no permit needed.
  • Re-roofing: a permit is needed only when sheathing is added or replaced.
  • Sheds: a permit is needed over 120 square feet, with one accessory building allowed per residential lot.
  • Fences: no permit at 6 feet or less, with 6-foot fences allowed in the rear yard and 4.5-foot solid fences in the front yard.

Code enforcement is the other side of this. The municipal code requires grass on residential lots under five acres to stay below 8 inches, vacant lots under five acres below 10 inches, and it bars accumulations of broken or worn-out items on any property. Inherited and vacant houses are where these notices tend to pile up, so cutting the grass and clearing the yard before showing is a low-cost step.

How are deeds recorded in Johnson County?

Deeds for Shawnee property are recorded by the Johnson County Register of Deeds. The county's published fee schedule lists $21.00 for recording a deed or mortgage and $17.00 for each additional page. A Mortgage Registration Fee Affidavit carries no charge, and the county says it adds no fee for eRecording.

In a cash sale the title company or closing attorney usually handles recording, so the seller rarely visits the office. It still helps to know that a deed with a missing page, or one that does not match the name on the record, is the kind of problem that slows a closing.

What is Shawnee Mission Park, and does it matter to sellers?

Shawnee Mission Park is a county park of more than 1,600 acres at West 79th Street and Renner Road, with a 120-acre lake. Johnson County Park and Recreation says it is the most visited park in Kansas.

The facility page lists 11 shelters, nature trails, an archery range, a dog off-leash area, disc golf and a swimming beach. A seller whose house sits near the park can name it in the description, since buyers search by the places they use.

What do Shawnee sellers usually run into?

The common situations are inherited houses, tenant-occupied rentals, deferred repairs and a sale on a deadline. In each one a cash offer removes the listing steps that eat time.

  • Inherited house: a probate or transfer step may come first, and the Johnson County tax bill keeps arriving in the meantime.
  • Tenant in place: showings are hard to schedule, and a buyer who accepts the property as it stands avoids that.
  • Repair backlog: a roof with failed sheathing, for example, can bring a permit into the picture.
  • Tax timing: a November bill or a May second half can land close to closing.

Whatever route you choose, collect the latest tax statement, the notice of appraised value and any city code letter before you start. Those three papers answer most of the questions a buyer or title company will have.

How many people live in Shawnee, Kansas?

The 2020 census counted 67,311 residents in Shawnee. The Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate, shown at the top of this page, is higher at 69,848.

What is the total property tax rate in Shawnee?

It depends on the school district. The city's 2027 budget presentation shows 106.066 mills for addresses in Shawnee Mission USD 512 and 117.222 mills for addresses in De Soto USD 232, based on 2026 budget-year levies.

When are Shawnee property taxes due?

Johnson County mails tax bills on November 15, and the first half or full payment is due December 20. The second half bill is mailed May 1 and is due May 10.

Do I need a permit to replace the roof on my Shawnee house?

Only if sheathing is being added or replaced. The city's FAQ says a re-roof without sheathing work does not need a permit, but structural changes, electrical upgrades and demolitions do.

Where do I appeal my Shawnee property value?

You file with the Johnson County Appraiser's Office, through its online portal or by mail to the office in Olathe. The deadline is 30 days after the notice was mailed, which the county lists as on or before March 31.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Johnson County?

The county's fee schedule lists $21.00 for the first page and $17.00 for each additional page. Confirm the current amount with the Register of Deeds before you rely on it.

What should a seller know about Manhattan, KS before choosing how to sell?

Manhattan is a college and Army town, and that mix sets the tone for most home sales here. The city is the county seat of Riley County, it reaches into Pottawatomie County, and the 2020 census counted 54,100 people.

Sellers usually weigh three paths: list with an agent, sell on your own, or take a cash offer. The sections below cover the local facts that change the answer, including water and weather, rental rules, taxes and deed paperwork.

Where is Manhattan and how is it laid out?

Manhattan sits in northeastern Kansas where the Big Blue River meets the Kansas River, about 50 miles west of Topeka. The original downtown was built on a broad, flat floodplain, while much of the city around it rolls into the Flint Hills.

Tuttle Creek Reservoir lies about five miles north of town, and the Konza Prairie preserve is to the south. Interstate 70 runs roughly nine miles south of the city, with three exits that feed Manhattan: K-177 at exit 313, McDowell Creek Road at exit 307 and K-18 at exit 303. US-24 crosses the city as Tuttle Creek Boulevard before turning toward Wamego. Manhattan Regional Airport, on K-18 about two miles west of town, has American Eagle service to Chicago O'Hare and Dallas/Fort Worth, and the ATA Bus runs fixed routes inside the city.

Manhattan ZIP codes are 66502, 66503, 66505 and 66506.

How did Manhattan grow into the Little Apple?

Manhattan began in 1855 when New England Free-State settlers arrived under the New England Emigrant Aid Company. A steamer carrying Ohio settlers from the Cincinnati-Manhattan Company ran aground in the Kansas River that June, and the combined town took the name Manhattan on June 29, 1855. It was incorporated on May 30, 1857.

Education drove the next chapter. The Kansas legislature established Kansas State Agricultural College in 1863, and it opened that September as the first public college in Kansas and the first land-grant institution under the Morrill Act. The Kansas Pacific Railroad reached the town in 1866. Every census since 1870 has recorded growth, from 1,173 residents then to 54,100 in 2020.

Who employs Manhattan residents?

Kansas State University is the leading employer, with more than 6,000 people working on campus, according to the Manhattan Area Chamber of Commerce. The chamber also points to Fort Riley, the National Bio and Agro-Defense Facility and Caterpillar Work Tools among the larger employers, and the city's 2026 budget book names Kansas State, Fort Riley, USD 383 and Ascension hospital.

The same budget book lists a Manhattan metro labor force of 65,170 with a 3.2% unemployment rate for December 2025.

  • Kansas State University: the campus workforce is the largest in the city.
  • Fort Riley: the 100,656-acre post sits between Manhattan and Junction City and is home to the 1st Infantry Division.
  • Manhattan-Ogden USD 383: the public school district that serves most of the city.
  • Ascension hospital and private employers such as CivicPlus.

What does Manhattan's flood history mean for a house sale?

Flood risk is the first environmental question many Manhattan buyers ask. The city was built at the downstream end of the Big Blue River watershed, and the Big Blue and Kansas Rivers Floodplain Management Plan, sponsored by the Army Corps of Engineers, the State of Kansas, the city and both counties, describes the south and east side of the city as carrying a particular flood risk.

The plan counts 43 flood events between 1904 and 1951. The 1951 flood led to Tuttle Creek Dam, finished in 1962, and the Manhattan Levee System, finished in 1963. The city later raised the levee and replaced original equipment from the 1960s. Residential areas along Casement Road and Marlatt Avenue are named in the plan as part of the studied floodplain, along with the commercial corridor on US-24 in Pottawatomie County.

For a seller, the practical steps are simple. Pull the flood zone for your parcel before you talk price, find out whether you carry flood insurance, and gather any elevation certificate or repair records.

How do Manhattan's tornado and temperature swings affect a house?

Manhattan has a humid continental climate, so roofs, siding and heating systems all work for their living. Average precipitation is 35.77 inches a year, and the temperature reaches 90 degrees or higher on about 59 days a year and 0 degrees or lower on about four days. Snowfall averages 17.6 inches.

The most destructive tornado on record hit at about 10:30 p.m. on June 11, 2008. The EF4 storm destroyed 31 homes and caused about $20 million in damage on the Kansas State campus. An earlier tornado on June 8, 1966 injured at least 65 people.

Manhattan also sits near the Nemaha Ridge, and the strongest earthquake to originate in Kansas, a magnitude 5.1 event, was centered here in 1867. It caused largely minor damage. The Army Corps of Engineers later finished a project in 2010 that replaced sand under the Tuttle Creek dam with more than 350 concrete walls.

The city has a rental registration program, and the program page says owners must register all rental units. Inspections are not mandatory under that program, but the Risk Reduction office, reachable at 785-587-4506, encourages owners to ask for one and offers a property maintenance checklist.

Riley County bills real estate taxes in arrears. The Treasurer's Office is at 110 Courthouse Plaza in Manhattan, and payments can also be made by phone at 785-377-5385.

Kansas runs the assessment calendar statewide. County appraisers mail valuation notices by March 1, taxpayers have 30 days from the mailing date to start an equalization appeal, and informal meetings with the appraiser run through May 15. If you sell mid-year, the tax bill for the year you are leaving is still coming, so ask the closing agent how the proration will be handled.

What deed paperwork does a Manhattan sale involve?

Kansas requires a real estate sales validation questionnaire with almost every deed that is recorded. Under K.S.A. 79-1437c, a deed cannot be recorded by the register of deeds unless the questionnaire is attached, and the office keeps it for five years before destroying it.

Some transfers are exempt, including gifts, sheriff's deeds and transfers by an executor under court order, and the exemption number must be written on the document itself. Title companies normally prepare this paperwork, so a seller mostly needs to confirm the price and the names on the deed are correct.

How does a cash sale compare with a listing in Manhattan?

A listing gives you the widest audience and the longest process: preparation, showings, buyer financing and the appraisal. A cash sale to a company like ours cuts out the lender, so the closing date is set by you and the title work rather than by a loan file.

Parts of it are. The city's own floodplain management plan describes flood risk along the Big Blue and Kansas Rivers, and the Manhattan Levee System protects areas of the city. Whether a specific parcel is in a mapped flood zone depends on its address, so check the parcel with the city before you set a price.

When are property taxes due in Riley County?

The first half is due by December 20 and the second half by May 10 of the following year, according to the Riley County Treasurer. When December 20 falls on a weekend, the postmark deadline moves, as it did to December 22 in 2025.

Do I need to register a rental house in Manhattan before I sell it?

The city requires owners to register rental units, and inspections are not part of that program. If the house has been a rental, confirm it is registered so a buyer or title agent does not raise it later.

What is the sales validation questionnaire?

It is a Kansas form that must accompany a deed when it is recorded, unless the transfer is exempt. It records the sale price and conditions for the state's valuation system, and the register of deeds keeps it for five years.

Can I sell a damaged Manhattan house as it is?

Yes. Owners with storm damage, flood damage or deferred repairs can sell without fixing the house first. The trade-off is that an as-is sale is priced for the work the buyer will take on, so compare it with what repairs and a listing would cost you.

Salina sits where Interstate 70 meets Interstate 135, at an elevation of 1,224 feet in the Smoky Hills region. It is 81 miles north of Wichita, 164 miles west of Kansas City, Missouri, and 401 miles east of Denver.

How did Salina begin?

Settlers from Lawrence founded the Salina Town Company in 1858 and named the town for the salty Saline River. The county was organized around it, and Salina incorporated as a city in 1870.

As the westernmost town on the Smoky Hill Trail, Salina grew as a trading post for emigrants, gold prospectors headed to Pikes Peak and area tribes. A second boom came in the 1940s and 1950s when the Smoky Hill Army Airfield was built. Lee Jeans opened its first garment factory in Salina in 1889.

What did the 1951 flood change in Salina?

In 1951 Salina experienced what the Army Corps of Engineers calls a 500-year flood. Afterward a federal levee system was built, and it cut off 6.8 miles of the Smoky Hill River's channel through downtown.

That old channel now receives runoff from a 4.6 square mile urban drainage rather than the 8,341 square miles it drained before. The city approved a Smoky Hill River Master Plan in 2010, and the Corps' restoration study lists design work from September 2026 to 2028, construction starting in 2028 and completion in 2030. If your house is near the river or the old channel, ask for the flood zone and any insurance history before setting a price.

What should Salina sellers know about tornadoes and hail?

Salina sits in a region prone to severe thunderstorms with damaging winds, hail and tornadoes. An F3 tornado struck the south part of the city on June 21, 1969, severely damaging or destroying more than 100 homes and businesses and injuring 60 people. Another F3 on September 25, 1973 passed through the southeast and destroyed two houses and a trailer park, and an EF3 passed the south side on June 11, 2008.

The climate numbers explain the wear on a house: the temperature reaches 90 degrees about 68 days a year and 100 degrees about 16 days, falls below freezing about 115 days, and the city gets about 32 inches of precipitation and 16.6 inches of snow. Roofs and siding here take real wear. If you have unrepaired storm damage, an as-is sale avoids a repair project.

Salina Regional Health Center is the largest employer in Saline County at 2,800 employees, according to a Salina Journal list drawn from the Salina Economic Development Organization. The hospital's own community page also names Schwan's Global Supply, described as the world's largest maker of frozen pizza, along with Exide Technology and Great Plains Manufacturing.

Manufacturing, education, health and social services lead the local economy, and agricultural transportation is a significant industry. The 7,000-seat Tony's Pizza Events Center hosts events. Kansas State University Polytechnic Campus, Kansas Wesleyan University and Salina Area Technical College are all located in the city.

Salina's property maintenance code sits in chapter 31 of its code of ordinances. If the house has a violation notice, deal with it before closing so the buyer does not inherit it.

A cash sale suits homes that need roof or storm repairs, estate properties, houses with tenants, and sellers working to a date. Listing may bring more buyers when a house is in good repair. Contact us with the address and we will give you an honest comparison.

Where is Hutchinson, Kansas, and how does the city sit on the land?

Hutchinson is the Reno County seat in south-central Kansas, at the meeting of U.S. 50 and K-96, about 39 miles northwest of Wichita. It lies on the northeast bank of the Arkansas River in the Great Bend Sand Prairie region, and Cow Creek, a tributary of the Arkansas, runs southeast through the city.

The city covers 22.69 square miles of land. That is roughly twice the land area of Garden City or Gardner, and it gives Hutchinson room for older neighborhoods near downtown, newer streets toward the edges, and industrial areas around the rail lines.

The Census Bureau estimates 39,595 residents as of July 1, 2025, a 1.0 percent drop from the April 2020 base of 40,007. Hutchinson has lost population slowly since 2010, when the census counted 42,080.

What is the story of Salt City?

Hutchinson was founded in 1871 by C.C. Hutchinson, who contracted with the Santa Fe Railway to place a town at the railroad's crossing of the Arkansas River. The town grew up about half a mile north on Cow Creek. In 1887, Ben Blanchard drilled for oil near here and found salt instead, and Hutchinson became known as Salt City.

  • The Carey Salt Company opened the only salt mine in Hutchinson in 1923, and the Hutchinson Salt Company runs it today.
  • Cargill and Morton Salt operate evaporative salt plants in the city.
  • Parts of the mined-out space are used for archival storage of film masters, data tapes and business records.
  • In 1913, Hutchinson gave the state the land that became the Kansas State Fairgrounds, and the fair has been held here ever since.

The salt history matters to a homeowner in one specific way. On January 17, 2001, natural gas leaked from the Yaggy storage field, traveled underground and surfaced through old brine wells. An explosion downtown destroyed two businesses and damaged 26 others, and a second blast the next day killed two people in a mobile home park. If a buyer asks about it, your title company and the county can help you pull the records for your parcel.

Which employers and institutions support Hutchinson's housing market?

Hutchinson's economy rests on salt, manufacturing, food distribution, health care and education. Wikipedia describes these anchors:

  • Dillon's grocery stores were established in Hutchinson in the 1920s, and the company still keeps a distribution center and the headquarters for Dillons and Kwik Shop here.
  • Eaton Corporation runs a hydraulics plant in the city.
  • Kuhn-Krause makes agricultural equipment in a large local plant.
  • Hutchinson Regional Medical Center is the larger of two hospitals.
  • Hutchinson Community College's main campus is in the city, beside the Cosmosphere.

Many households stay put for years. The Census Bureau finds that 80.9 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and the median household income is $58,687.

Hutchinson has the lowest median home value among the four Kansas cities in this guide series, so the dollar gap between a repair bill and a house's value can be narrower here.

How does Hutchinson's weather affect a house?

Hutchinson has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters. Temperatures exceed 90 degrees on an average of 63.4 afternoons a year and fall below freezing on 119.5 mornings. Precipitation averages 32.93 inches, and May is the wettest month.

The extremes have been sharp. Hutchinson hit 113 degrees on July 27, 2011, and fell to minus 19 on February 16, 2021, the coldest reading on record in the city.

Yes. Ordinance 2019-17 requires every residential rental unit in the city to be licensed each year. A unit not licensed by the May 31 deadline is in violation, an administration fee of $20 a month applies for each month it is rented unlicensed, and operating an unlicensed unit is a Class C misdemeanor under the ordinance.

The ordinance also sets up a voluntary interior inspection program. Landlords or tenants can request an inspection from the Inspections Department, and results are posted on the city's website. Units in good standing that pass a requested inspection can earn 'best-practice rental' status, which carries a 50 percent license fee reduction for three calendar years.

If you are selling a rental house, confirm the license is current before closing so the buyer does not inherit a fee or a violation. Check the city's website for the current ordinance text, since it may have been amended.

How do roads, transit and schools work in Hutchinson?

Three public districts serve the area: Hutchinson USD 308, Nickerson-South Hutchinson USD 309 and Buhler USD 313. USD 308 operates eight elementary schools, two middle schools, Hutchinson High School and a career and technical academy in the city.

  • U.S. 50 runs east-west south of the city, K-96 bypasses it on the west, and K-61 runs through the east side.
  • Reno County Area Transit runs three bus routes, called Red, Blue and Yellow.
  • Amtrak's Southwest Chief stops here, and Wichita's airport handles most commercial flights.

Because Hutchinson sits 39 miles from Wichita, some buyers commute to jobs in the larger city. A house with an easy route to U.S. 50 or K-96 has that selling point.

What offices and deadlines matter when you sell in Hutchinson?

The Reno County Appraiser, Register of Deeds and Treasurer all work from 125 W. 1st Avenue in downtown Hutchinson. That is helpful on closing week, since a recorded deed, a tax question and a parcel record can be sorted out in one trip.

  • Tax calendar. The county treasurer mails statements on or after November 1. The first half is due by December 20 and the second half by May 10, and a variable interest penalty accrues after that.
  • Protests. An owner who has not appealed before can file a protest form with the treasurer by December 20, or by January 31 if a lender pays the tax from escrow.
  • Unpaid tax. The county says a residential property has three years to redeem after unpaid tax begins running, or it can be sold at tax foreclosure auction, usually in the fall.
  • Deeds. Most deeds need a sales validation questionnaire under K.S.A. 79-1437c.

If you owe back taxes, tell the buyer and title company at the start. Ask the title company how any unpaid balance will be handled at closing.

Common situations include a home that needs a lot of work relative to its value, a rental with a tenant, an estate, and a move to be near family.

  • Inherited property. Heirs may live far away and want to avoid paying taxes and utilities on an empty house.
  • Smaller buyer pool for homes needing work. A financed buyer's appraisal can flag repairs the lender will not fund.

The Reno County Register of Deeds sets fees under state law (K.S.A. 28-115), and the amount depends on the number of pages. Call the office at 125 W. 1st Avenue or ask your title company to quote the fee before closing.

The license is required to rent the unit, not to sell it. Hutchinson's ordinance charges $20 a month for each month an unlicensed unit is rented after the May 31 deadline, so bring the license current before closing.

Can I sell a Hutchinson house that has unpaid property taxes?

Yes. Unpaid taxes are paid from sale proceeds at closing. Reno County says unpaid real estate tax can lead to tax foreclosure and auction after a redemption period, which is three years for residential property, so do not wait.

Leavenworth, founded in 1854, was the first city incorporated in the Kansas Territory. It grew south of Fort Leavenworth, which began in 1827 as Cantonment Leavenworth under Colonel Henry Leavenworth.

That figure means most Leawood houses are already built, and sellers compete with other resale homes more than with new lots.

The population history shows a city that has largely filled in. Census counts were 27,656 in 2000, 31,867 in 2010 and 33,902 in 2020, and the 6.4 percent growth in the last decade was the slowest of any decade in the census table. Modern Leawood began in the 1920s, when Oscar G. Lee moved to Johnson County and oversaw the building of Lee Boulevard. The city is named for him. A housing development by the Kroh Brothers led to incorporation on November 30, 1948, when Leawood was a third-class city with fewer than 2,000 people. The Kroh Brothers modeled their neighborhoods on those of Kansas City developer J. C. Nichols, who used curving streets, uniform architecture, extensive deed restrictions and homes associations. Most Leawood neighborhoods have homeowners associations, so the city's rules and the association's rules both apply. The city's Neighborhood Services office enforces a Property Maintenance Code covering premise condition, paint, roof overhangs, gutters and exterior structure condition.

The Dodge City Town Company staked its claim in August 1872, a month before the Santa Fe survey reached the area. A City of Dodge City planning document says shipments rose from 9,540 head of cattle in the first season, 1876, to 65,000 head by 1882.

The cattle trade moved on, but the town kept its role as county seat and distribution point. The same document says the city's population rose from 11,252 in 1950 to 25,176 in 2000. The later growth came with meatpacking: Excel Corporation of Wichita opened a plant on the east edge of town in 1980, and Cargill later acquired it. The small HyPlains plant was bought by National Beef.

The planning document also notes floods in 1942 and 1965 that led to federal flood control works along what is now a dry Arkansas River bed. For a house, that history is a reminder to check flood maps rather than assume a dry riverbed means no risk.

Meat packing is the primary industry in Dodge City, and both Cargill Meat Solutions and National Beef run large facilities here. Wikipedia adds that the city also has farm implement manufacturing, serves as a supply center for area agriculture, and has a tourism sector tied to its Old West identity.

The Golden Triangle of Meat-packing article on Wikipedia ties Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal together as three southwestern Kansas cities whose populations grew from 1980 to 2020 on the strength of packing plant jobs. The article's table shows Ford County growing from 24,315 residents in 1980 to 34,287 in 2020, so the plants help shape who is looking for housing here.

Dodge City has hot summers and highly variable winters, and Wikipedia says it sits where semi-arid and humid subtropical climates meet. High temperatures reach 90 degrees an average of 71 days a year and 100 degrees on average 14 days a year.

The same article says severe weather, including tornadoes, is common, especially in spring, and that Dodge City is often cited as the windiest city in the United States, with an average wind speed of 13.9 mph. On who pays the year's tax, the Kansas statute K.S.A. 79-1805, as described on the Pottawatomie County website, makes the buyer responsible for real property sold on or after January 1 and before November 1, and the seller responsible for a sale between November 1 and January 1, unless the contract says otherwise. Inside the city, building work goes through Development Services and Inspections, which includes planning and zoning, building inspections and code enforcement. The city's main number is 620-225-8100.

The city's historical essay says Boot Hill Museum began in 1931, and that the film Dodge City premiered in town on April 1, 1939. Tourism still plays a part in the local economy, including a casino resort that Wikipedia describes. Visitors may notice the smell of feedlots and packing plants, a point the same city document makes about the modern town.

Ford County. The appraiser values the property, and the county treasurer bills it. Taxes are due December 20, with the second half due May 10.

Where is Garden City, Kansas, and how is the city laid out?

Garden City is a city in southwestern Kansas, on the north side of the Arkansas River in the High Plains, at the crossing of U.S. Route 50 and U.S. Route 83. It is the Finney County seat. Garden City was settled in 1878 by the Fulton brothers and grew after irrigation reached Finney County in 1879 through the Garden City Ditch. The Santa Fe railroad agreed to place a station here, and the land office followed, which brought a rush of homesteaders in the 1880s.

The next big change came in the 1970s, when the city council allowed a meatpacking plant. New workers arrived from Mexico, Vietnam, Myanmar, Somalia and other places, and the population climbed from 18,256 in 1980 to 28,451 in 2000. Storms are the larger risk to a roof. The city sits in Tornado Alley, and an F3 tornado struck the north side on June 23, 1967, damaging more than 400 homes. On April 30 and May 1, 2017, a late snowstorm cut power and damaged almost every tree in town, and one clinic roof collapsed.

Gardner at a glance

Selling in Gardner?

Get My Cash Offer →

Where is Gardner, Kansas, and what is the city like?

Gardner is a Johnson County city in the southwest corner of the Kansas City metro area. The Census Bureau lists 26,154 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 12.0 percent from the April 2020 base of 23,349.

The city covers about 10 square miles. Gardner Lake sits on the north side of town off South Gardner Road and 151st Street, and the headwaters of Kill Creek, which runs north to join the Kansas River at De Soto, are also here.

Gardner is also a commuter town. The Census Bureau puts the mean trip to work at 22.9 minutes, and 78.3 percent of residents 16 and older are in the labor force.

How did Gardner grow from a trail junction into a suburb?

Gardner was founded in 1857 as a Free-Stater settlement where the Santa Fe Trail split from the Oregon and California Trails. It was named for Henry Gardner, then governor of Massachusetts, and its first post office opened in 1858.

For most of the twentieth century it stayed small, with 676 people in 1950. Growth came later:

YearPopulation
19903,191
20009,396
201019,123
202023,287

The population grew from 3,191 in 1990 to 23,287 in 2020, so much of the housing was probably built in a short span and many homes may share similar ages and building systems. A seller whose roof, water heater and furnace were all installed around the same time may face several replacements in the same few years, which can weigh on a sale.

Which employers and schools shape Gardner's housing demand?

The school district is the largest local employer. USD 231 employs 926 people, according to the city's 2024 financial report as summarized on Wikipedia.

  • Unified School District 231: 926 employees
  • Walmart: 225
  • Cosentino's Price Chopper: 191
  • Meadowbrook Rehabilitation Hospital: 189
  • Excelligence Learning Corp: 175
  • City of Gardner: 165

Many residents work elsewhere in the metro. A BNSF Railway fueling plant and office opened in nearby Edgerton, about 3 miles from western Gardner, in May 2013 and employs about 200.

USD 231 runs six of its seven elementary schools inside Gardner, along with Wheatridge, Trail Ridge and Pioneer Ridge middle schools and Gardner Edgerton High School. Families often start a house search with the school boundaries, so a seller should know which elementary school serves the address.

What do Census numbers say about Gardner housing?

Gardner has the highest owner-occupancy rate and the highest median home value among the four Kansas cities in this guide series. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates are below.
